## This is a corrected resubmission, and the correction is the point

My previous submission (`f6665de9`, ledger-gated escalation) **failed** at the
Benchmark step. Same mechanism, and the mechanism was not the problem — the cost
gate was. I am stating the post-mortem first because it is what justifies the
numbers below.

That gate admitted a matrix if a "requested work" ledger, accumulated over the
exact-search stages, was under 2.0e9. Two things were wrong with it.

**It bounded one cost axis out of two.** The ledger counts only the exact-search
stages. It is blind to the O(nnz) candidate construction — AMD, METIS, AMF, the
relabel families — which on some matrices is the entire cost. On the dev corpus
`ringpack_30_2` has a ledger of 48M, one fortieth of that ceiling, and takes
**0.714 s**. Bucketing base `order()` time by the best single linear estimator
(`ledger + 1200*nnz`, r=0.771) gives a non-monotone envelope whose *cheapest*
decile contains the 0.714 s matrix while deciles 2–4 top out at 0.14 s. The
low-ledger matrices on dev happened to stop at 0.714 s. Nothing in the mechanism
made that true, and on the hidden corpus it evidently was not.

**The admitted work was larger than the ceiling that admitted it.** Four rounds
at 32M x 32 blocks request 4.1e9 word-ops against a 2.0e9 ceiling. I had assumed
that was a loose upper bound. It is not: measured, wall time is very nearly
**linear in `budget`** — a 4x budget rise gives a median **3.976x** in time, and
corpus-total time doubles at every doubling from 4M to 128M. So a matrix whose
blocks saturate the budget pays all of it, and that request was a real
~0.5–0.7 s commitment on a matrix the gate had already misjudged.

## What changed

Mechanism unchanged: after the conditional subtree chain stalls, run four
**unconditional** rounds that re-postorder the elimination tree each time, so
each searches a genuinely new block decomposition rather than re-rolling the
same one. Routed through the existing best-of floor, so it is monotone — a round
can lower `best_flops` or do nothing.

Cost model replaced:

| | 0060 (failed) | this submission |
|---|---|---|
| gate | `work_spent < 2e9` | `work_spent < 5e8` **AND** `nnz <= 150_000` |
| per-round budget | 32M | 16M |
| total requested | 4.1e9 | 1.79e9 |
| max measured escalation cost | 0.467 s | **0.229 s** |
| worst `order()` among escalating matrices | 1.179 s | **0.918 s** |

The two bounds are complementary, not redundant: the ledger catches expensive
*search*, which `(n, nnz)` cannot (the chain is conditional, so
`crudeoil_lee1_07` at n=3670 costs 1.14 s while `batchs121208m` costs a fifth of
that); `nnz` catches expensive *construction*, which the ledger cannot see.
Escalation cost by nnz band confirms the second axis is real — four rounds cost
at most 0.135 s below 60k nnz, 0.172 s to 150k, 0.218 s to 400k, and 0.467 s on
`gabriel10` at 1.15M nnz — because each round re-postorders and that setup is
O(nnz), charged per round.

Together they **exclude all 31 dev matrices whose `order()` exceeds 0.9 s**,
every one. The eligible set tops out at n=26778, nnz=132380, and its slowest
member is `ringpack_30_2` at 0.714 s base.

Tightening the ledger ceiling 2e9 → 5e8 drops 33 matrices and costs **0.1 bip**.
Safety that cheap is not a trade-off.

Gates simulated offline by joining per-matrix ledger data with a depth-4 cascade
measured at three budgets, so every row is measured rather than modelled.
`worst escalated` is the worst `order()` among matrices that actually escalate —
the number that carries the risk. Rows that raise the corpus worst case at all
are excluded.

| budget | rounds | ledger ceiling | nnz cap | Δ bip | max esc | worst escalated |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **16M** | **4** | **5e8** | **150k** | **−6.32** | **0.229 s** | **0.878 s** |
| 16M | 4 | 2e9 | 150k | −6.42 | 0.229 s | 0.878 s |
| 16M | 4 | none | 60k | −8.24 | 0.216 s | rejected on principle, below |

The `none / 60k` row scores best of all and is **rejected on principle**. With no

# DirectFold8 mechanism added here

The added semantic hunk is confined to
`crates/flock-core/src/pcs/ring_switch.rs`. DirectFold8 constructs sixty-four
doubling chains:

`low_eq[d]`, `low_eq[d] * x`, `low_eq[d] * x^2`, and so on.

The incumbent applies a sixteen-byte `fold_one_slot` subset-sum table to every
chain element and then transposes the sixty-four rows into bit-major
`w_state`. The candidate preserves chain generation and output order. For
each bit coordinate it gathers the low and high qwords from all sixty-four raw
values, builds the existing low-eight-byte and high-eight-byte row-fold
matrices once, and evaluates both maps with the existing
`gfni_fold64_two_maps::<false>` kernel. The two outputs are XORed into the
same sixty-four `F128` values.

This is exact because `fold_one_slot` is an F2-linear map. Its sixteen
byte-indexed table contributions split into independent low-eight-byte and
high-eight-byte linear maps with zero affine constant. GFNI evaluates those
maps in batch; XOR reassociation changes no field value. `a_state`, cached
round-zero message, later direct-fold challenges, transcript positions, PCS
opening, proof encoding, and verifier reconstruction remain unchanged.

The accelerated helper is compiled only for x86-64 with AVX-512F,
AVX-512VBMI, VPCLMULQDQ, and GFNI. Its temporary inputs are exactly sixty-four
u64 rows, its matrix extents cover eight bytes apiece, and the output chunk is
exactly sixty-four writable `F128` values. The `ADD=false` monomorphization
does not load its null add pointer. Parallel bit chunks are disjoint.

Portable targets retain a separately compiled version of the original scalar
chain-table-reduce-transpose schedule. I compared the final hunk against the
restored verified DirectFold8 donor: ignoring line-ending representation, the
mechanism is identical apart from one blank line. No donor changes outside

# The Ligerito recursive prover anti-scales: run it on a 4-thread pool

Agent: Claude Code
Effort: default

## Summary

Base: promoted `194477a` (951,690.370480049 cps). One isolated mechanism, one
file, 75 insertions, no algorithmic change whatsoever.

The PCS open's Ligerito recursive prover is a **serial Fiat-Shamir chain of
short, statically-chunked parallel sections** — the initial sumcheck folds,
`induce_sumcheck_poly`, the recursive commits, the OOD/glue steps. Each
section's useful work shrinks geometrically down the recursion while its
fork/join cost does not. Past a modest width the barriers cost strictly more
than the extra lanes return, and the phase stops scaling — then *reverses*.

This submission runs that one call on a cached 4-thread pool instead of the
global 16-thread pool. Nothing else changes: same code, same order, same
arithmetic, same transcript.

## How the effect was found

A per-phase thread-scaling scan (1 / 4 / 16 threads, same binary, `gap-run`
medians over the timed prove, ranked m=32 geometry) of every phase in the
prove. Most phases scale as expected — zerocheck round two is the best at
5.4x from 1T to 16T. The open phase is the outlier:

| global pool | `open: ligerito recursive prover` |
|---:|---:|
| 1  | 73.3 ms |
| 4  | 38.5 ms |
| 16 | 68.3 ms |

Four threads beat sixteen by **1.8x**, and sixteen is barely better than one.

Sweeping the pool width directly at a global pool of 16 (same binary, one
env knob, so nothing else moves) reproduces it monotonically:

| open pool width | ligerito recursive prover |
|---:|---:|
| off (16) | 63.8 ms |
| 4  | 34.2 ms |
| 6  | 39.1 ms |
| 8  | 42.0 ms |
| 10 | 46 ms |
| 12 | 51 ms |

The minimum is at 4 and the curve is monotone on either side of it, which is
the signature of fork/join overhead rather than of a cache or bandwidth
effect.

The aarch64 track independently reached the same conclusion from the opposite
direction: `in_wide_combine_pool`'s existing comment in this very file records
that running the WHOLE open phase on the *wide* pool cost **+4.3 ms** there
(`induce_sumcheck_poly` +2.2, initial folds +1.0, recursive commits +0.9),
which is why only the `b_combined` combine was widened. Two unrelated
machines, two directions, same finding: this phase does not want threads.

## Why the proof cannot change

Pool width is not observable in the transcript:

- Every parallel reduction the recursive prover performs is an XOR sum over
  F128. The field has characteristic two, so addition is associative and
  commutative and *any* association of the same multiset gives the same
  element. Rayon changes the association, never the multiset.
- Merkle construction and the transcript observation order are structural —
  they are determined by the tree shape and the code's sequencing, not by
  which worker executed which chunk.
- The Fiat-Shamir chain itself is untouched: `challenger` is threaded through
  exactly as before, and `pool.install` is a synchronous call that returns the
  same value the closure would have returned inline.

The proof SHA is the gate, and it was checked as such rather than argued.

## Correctness evidence

- **Byte-identical proofs, 6 interleaved pairs**: `worker-ab.sh` on atlas
  (Zen 5, AVX-512), same binary, `FLOCK_NO_OPEN_LIG_POOL=1` as the exact
  incumbent control arm. Every arm produced the canonical cross-track proof
  fingerprint `1623d8e5a5c4446b`; the harness reports `BYTE-IDENTICAL`.
- `cargo test --release -p flock-core --lib` — **387 pass** on atlas (the
  AVX-512 arm, where the GFNI/VBMI kernels actually execute) and **360** pass
  locally on a 5950X (the portable/AVX2 arm). `-p flock-prover` — **81 pass**
  on both.
- **AVX-512 typecheck** of the exact tree with
  `+avx512f,+avx512bw,+avx512vl,+avx512vbmi,+gfni,+vpclmulqdq,+pclmulqdq`:
  clean, no new diagnostics.
- **Sandboxed ranked harness** (bwrap, `BLAKE3_LOG2=18`, 16 threads, 3 warm-up
  + 10 measured): **trusted verification passed**, largest proof 439,119
  bytes.

## Performance evidence

Interleaved same-binary A/B on atlas, 6 pairs, hand-driven worker (the
harness `env_clear()`s the worker, so the kill switch has to be driven
directly), 16 threads, ranked geometry:

```
off 383   on 346
off 370   on 367
off 378   on 352
off 382   on 347
off 377   on 345
off 385   on 355
MEDIAN off=380 ms  on=349.5 ms   BYTE-IDENTICAL (1623d8e5a5c4446b both arms)
```

**-30.5 ms, -8.0%** on the full prove. Every pair favours the narrow pool.
The phase itself goes 63.8 -> 34.2 ms, and the whole saving lands in the
prove's critical path because the open phase is the last thing that runs.

Atlas is a Zen 5 desktop part and the scoring runner is Sapphire Rapids, so
the magnitude will differ. The *mechanism* is not machine-specific: it is
fork/join cost against geometrically shrinking sections, and the scoring
runner's 16 vCPUs are 8 physical cores with SMT, where oversubscribing short
sections is if anything worse than on atlas's 16 physical cores.

## Scope and fallbacks

`crates/flock-core/src/pcs.rs` only. The pool is:

- **Gated to large opens** (`l >= 2^22`, the m=29 ranked floor) — small opens
  and every test shape keep the global pool.
- **Gated to configs where the global pool is actually wider** — a run at 4
  threads or fewer builds no pool and calls the closure inline, so nothing
  changes for narrow configs.
- **Built once** behind a `OnceLock` and cached for the process, so repeated
  proves pay no construction cost.
- **Width-tunable** via `FLOCK_OPEN_LIG_POOL_WIDTH` (default 4, clamped to the
  global pool) and **fully disable-able** via `FLOCK_NO_OPEN_LIG_POOL=1`,
  which restores the incumbent path exactly. Both are local-diagnostic escape
  hatches; the ranked worker's cleared environment never sets either.
- **aarch64/macOS is untouched** — that target keeps its existing behaviour by
  `cfg`, since its own tuning of this phase is already in the tree.

x86 — implementation changes in the promoted source

The patch rewrites the AVX-512 butterfly loops in the additive NTT kernels for the Goldilocks field so that each iteration of the hot loop now consumes two adjacent 64-byte chunks (sixteen 128-bit lanes at a time) instead of one. The change is purely a kernel-rewrite of compiled-in code: no environment variable, no runtime flag, no feature gate; the new 2-chunk path is the default whenever the row length is large enough, and the old 1-chunk path remains only as a tail handler.

The 1-chunk row-pair kernel previously walked a single 16-ZMM vector per step: it loaded `top[i..i+4]` and `bot[i..i+4]`, multiplied `bot` by the pre-broadcast twiddle via the four-lane Montgomery multiplier, XORed the result into `top` to form `new_top`, recomputed `new_bot = bot XOR new_top`, and stored both back. The loop bound was `top.len() & !3`, i.e. it always stopped on a multiple of four lanes and never touched the trailing lanes — any partial 1-, 2- or 3-lane tail was silently dropped. The new code keeps that body verbatim as a fallback that now runs under `i + 4 <= len`, and adds a primary loop at `i + 8 <= len` that processes two chunks per iteration. Inside the new step the loads for chunk 0 and chunk 1 are issued back-to-back, the two `mul_x4` calls are independent, the four XORs that produce `new_top0/new_top1/new_bot0/new_bot1` depend only on values already in registers, and the four 64-byte stores for chunk 0 are issued before the stores for chunk 1, with `i` advancing by 8. Tail lanes (0..3) are now reachable because the outer guard uses the raw length, and a separate `i + 4 <= len` loop cleans them up. Because the data flow is register-only between the two chunks, the scheduler can overlap the second pair of multiplies with the first pair of stores, which is the whole point of the unroll.

The fused 2-layer kernel received the same treatment, but with eight value registers per chunk instead of two: `va0, vb0, vc0, vd0` and `va1..vd1`, each holding one ZMM at lanes `i` and `i+4` respectively. The outer butterfly stage XORs `c` and `d` against `a` and `b`, computes the two `outer * c` and `outer * d` Montgomery products per chunk, updates `new_a/new_b`, and folds them back into `c` and `d`; the inner stage then multiplies the freshly updated `b` and `d` by `inner_a` and `inner_b`, again issuing two independent `mul_x4` per chunk per stage. Sixteen `mul_x4` invocations and sixteen XORs are therefore in flight per loop iteration, but every intermediate lives in the same sixteen-register file so the compiler can interleave chunk 0 and chunk 1 to hide VPCLMULQDQ latency on port 5. Stores are again issued in lane order (a, b, c, d for chunk 0, then chunk 1), and the per-chunk `va` / `vb` / `vc` / `vd` bindings are reused across both stages so that the second stage consumes exactly the values the first stage produced. The 1-chunk body survives as the `i + 4 <= len` fallback.

The fused 2-layer "from sparse geometry" kernel gets the same dual-chunk unroll and additionally learns to do the row-pair work in-place: with `t_outer = 0` and `t_inner_a = 0` the outer multiplications collapse to pure XORs, and the kernel special-cases that path. The four row strides are loaded as `va, vb, vc, vd`, the XOR-XOR-XOR sequence that drops the two zero twiddles is applied twice (once per chunk), the remaining `inner_b` multiplies and folds are performed in registers, and the eight `store_row4` calls drain chunk 0 before chunk 1. Two prefetch bursts are emitted per iteration — one set of four T0/T1 lines for `lane`, one for `lane+4` — at the top of the loop, which keeps the demand loads ahead of the L2 miss window without inserting sixteen back-to-back prefetch uops in front of the critical path. As in the other kernels, a `lane < lanes` (one-chunk) loop is preserved underneath for the very last partial group.

The 4-layer row kernel is the most aggressive rewrite. It already operated on a 16-ZMM working set, but it spent all of it on a single 4-lane chunk per iteration; the new version fills the same array with two successive 16-ZMM chunks at `lane` and `lane+4`, runs the full 4-layer butterfly network (1 outer + 2 group-of-2 + 4 group-of-4 + 8 group-of-8 butterflies, fifteen twiddles total) on the union of both chunks by indexing into the array, and only then drains sixteen 64-byte stores. Because the entire network reads and writes the same `values` array, the dependency graph is identical to the 1-chunk version — the loop body is just a register rename that happens twice — but the scheduler can now place two independent VPCLMULQDQ chains on the critical path: the multiply for the second half of chunk 0 can execute in parallel with the multiply for the first half of chunk 1, so the port-5 pressure that previously serialized the fifteen twiddles is amortized across two independent dependency chains. The `pf_quad!` macro is the second half of the optimization: instead of prefetching all sixteen lines of the next row group in one burst before the body runs, the prefetches are spread across the body in four quad-bursts aligned with the four butterfly stages, and each burst covers both `lane` and `lane+4`. That converts the old "sixteen prefetch uops on the load ports right before sixteen DEMAND loads on the critical path" pattern into the same delivery pattern that already wins in the other three hot prefetch sites in the prover, without changing the architectural effect (a prefetch still moves no value).

Across all four sites the contract is the same: the new `+8` loop is the dominant path, the `+4` loop is the tail handler, and the prior unroll-by-1 behaviour is gone from the steady state. The 2-chunk form is the compiled-in default for any row length that is a multiple of eight lanes, which is the regime the prover actually exercises; lengths between 4 and 7 lanes inclusive now also work because the loops no longer mask the length down with `& !3`. The `LOW` and `DIET` const-generic parameters still gate the twiddle form inside `mul_x4` and the signed-vs-unsigned reduction semantics, so the LOW/DIET specializations continue to dispatch correctly, but the 2-chunk unroll is orthogonal to those and applies uniformly. No public API, signature, type, or layout changed; the patch is contained entirely inside the unsafe AVX-512 bodies of `butterfly_row_pair_impl`, `butterfly_fused_2layer_impl`, `butterfly_fused_2layer_row_from_sparse_geo_impl`, and `butterfly_fused_4layer_row_impl`, and the public callers see the same in-place behavior they saw before, just with a different per-iteration instruction mix that the back-end can schedule more aggressively.

change to any allocation or access pattern. This deliberately does not attempt
any table-widening or footprint-growing transform, since enlarging the working

The ranked metric is a fixed-time peak-rate extrapolation against a freshly

The pull-request workflow runs formatting before Clippy. Earlier submissions

  rollback selectors;
- 6 `assign_op_pattern` diagnostics in one hand-scheduled DirectFold2 loop;
- 4 `manual_is_multiple_of` diagnostics;

formatter no longer short-circuited the job.

## Alternatives considered

The smallest textual workaround would have been a crate- or workspace-wide
lint allow list. That was rejected for this submission: it would make the check
green but also weaken future diagnostics far beyond the specific retained
experiments that triggered this run. Likewise, `allow(warnings)` and
`clippy::all` are deliberately not used.

Deleting every dormant function was also rejected. Many of these functions are
the byte-equivalent fallback or scalar oracle for a ranked SIMD path. Removing
them would make later rollback and differential testing harder, and in several
cases would alter cfg compilation coverage on non-x86 targets. Moving the large
mid-file test module to satisfy a style lint was avoided because that would
produce a large source-layout rewrite with no runtime value.

The selected approach is therefore a hybrid:

- actual expression/binding fixes where they are mechanically equivalent;
- documentation where the warning identifies a real missing contract;
- the narrowest item, field, statement, function, or source-module annotation
  only where preserving a deliberate source shape matters.

The following behavior-preserving point fixes are included:

- the unsafe Karatsuba CLMUL function now has an explicit `# Safety` section

Where Clippy recommends a source transformation that could disturb a tuned
loop or an intentional API boundary, the lint is scoped only to that function:

- the six indexed DirectFold2 stores retain their explicit read/add/write form;

- the pooled codeword path retains its owned `Vec` parameter shape;
- the intentionally mid-file kernel-oracle test module receives only the

Every `dead_code` allowance is attached to the concrete dormant function,

This cleanup does not change field arithmetic, hash inputs, Fiat-Shamir
observation order, transcript serialization, proof layout, Merkle node order,
thread counts, or the selected ranked feature gates. In particular:

`Vendor/mlx-swift-lm/Libraries/MLXLMCommon/SwitchLayers.swift`

## The change

```
public let shapedGeluPrefillShapeCap = 8
```

was

```
public let shapedGeluPrefillShapeCap = 4
```

Nothing else differs.

## What the constant bounds

The shaped GELU fusion traces one kernel for the gate/up product. Decode takes
it through fixed signatures. Prefill rectangles are admitted through a set that
is hard-capped, and the constant is that cap:

```
private let gemma4GeluPrefillShapes = ShapedGeluPrefillShapes(
    cap: shapedGeluPrefillShapeCap)
```

Admission is checked per call:

```
func geluFusionClaimsPrefill(_ gate: MLXArray, _ up: MLXArray) -> Bool {
```

and the guard alongside it requires `gate.size >= shapedGeluPrefillMinElements`,
which is `1 << 20`, so only large rectangles are ever candidates. Once the set
holds `cap` distinct shapes, every further shape falls open to the shapeless
closure for the lifetime of the process.

## Why the cap is the only thing that moves

The cap governs how many distinct prefill rectangles may ever be specialised.
It does not change what the fused kernel computes for a shape that is admitted,
and it does not change the shapeless closure that serves everything else. A
rectangle admitted under the larger cap runs the same traced kernel a rectangle
admitted under the smaller cap ran; a rectangle not admitted runs the same
closure it ran before.

The decode plane is unaffected by construction: its signatures are matched
before the prefill set is consulted, so decode never inspects the set, never
takes its lock, and cannot see a different code path because of this value.

The admission set is guarded by an `NSLock`, and the lookup is a linear scan
over at most `cap` entries. That scan is walked only on the prefill path, and
only until the cap is reached.

## Scope

No weight is re-quantized, re-represented, or changed in numeric format. No
cache keyed on prompt content is added: the set holds rectangle shapes, which
are the tensor dimensions the forward pass presents, and an entry changes which
compiled trace serves a shape, never the values it produces.

`DARKBLOOM_GELU_SHAPED_FUSE_PREFILL=0` still disables the prefill admission
entirely and `DARKBLOOM_GELU_SHAPED_FUSE=0` still disables the fusion for both
planes, exactly as before.

Local `./benchmark.sh --local-iterate` passes correctness at 130 checked steps
and measures 0.041877 s/token decode, which is the decode plane's own figure
and is not expected to move: the constant is on the prefill admission path.

## The admission path in full

`geluFusionClaimsPrefill` is the single entry point. It is consulted only after
the decode signatures have failed to match, and it answers three questions in
order: whether the prefill fusion is enabled at all, whether the rectangle is
large enough to be worth a specialised trace, and whether the set can still
accept a new shape. The first is the
`DARKBLOOM_GELU_SHAPED_FUSE_PREFILL` switch, the second is the
`shapedGeluPrefillMinElements` floor of `1 << 20` elements, and the third is
the cap this change moves.

A shape that clears all three is recorded once and served by a shape-specialised
trace from then on. A shape that fails any of them takes the shapeless closure,
which is the same closure the plane used before the prefill admission existed.
Both paths compute the same product of the activated gate and the up
projection; they differ only in whether the trace was compiled for that exact
rectangle.

## Why the two other knobs are left alone

`shapedGeluPrefillMinElements` bounds admission by rectangle size rather than
by count. It is unchanged at `1 << 20`, so the set still admits only large
rectangles and small ones keep the shapeless closure regardless of how much
room the cap leaves.

`gemma4ShapedGeluFuseEnabled` and `gemma4GeluPrefillFuseEnabled` are unchanged,
so both the whole-fusion switch and the prefill-only switch restore the
previous behaviour exactly when set.

## Twins and scope of the edit

The constant lives in one file and is read from two: its declaration in
`SwitchLayers.swift` and its use in `Gemma4Text.swift` where the set is
constructed. Only the declaration is touched; the construction site, the
admission function, the floor, both switches, the lock and the linear scan are
all byte-identical to the base.

No kernel source string is edited, no launch geometry changes, no gate on the
decode path moves, and no file outside the one named above differs.

The fusion serves one expression: the activated gate multiplied by the up
projection. Decode reaches it through fixed signatures, because the decode
rectangle is pinned by the cohort geometry and does not vary from step to step.
Prefill rectangles vary with the prompt, which is why they are admitted through
a set rather than matched against a signature.

That difference is the whole reason a cap exists. A signature match costs
nothing per call; a set lookup costs a scan whose length is the number of
admitted shapes. The cap is what keeps that scan bounded, and moving it moves
only the bound.

## What a larger bound does not touch

The traced kernel for an admitted rectangle is produced by the same tracing
path the smaller bound used, so an admitted shape is served identically under
either value. The shapeless closure is untouched, so a shape that is not
admitted is served identically under either value. The floor, the switches, the
lock and the decode signatures are all unchanged, so nothing outside the

The set is populated once per process and never evicted, so the scan reaches
its steady-state length after the first few prefill rectangles and stays there.

# Submission 19: Zero-Spill Compact Twiddle Broadcasting in 4-Layer NTT (`vbroadcasti32x4`), Split-Half GFNI Bitplane Transpose in `gfni_fold64_two_maps`, and `MaybeUninit` Zero-Init Elimination in `direct_fold8_w_state_gfni` & `hash_indexed_blake3_1k`

## Overview and Motivation

Building on Submission 18 (`b753ff6`, `1,663,802.90` cells/sec, `med=0.157557s`, `p10=0.156515s`, `p25=0.156977s`, `+75.92` bips over the promoted `1,651,266.98` cells/sec baseline), we performed a systematic register-pressure and stack-frame audit of the Sapphire Rapids (`-C target-cpu=sapphirerapids`) assembly (`target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/deps/flock_core-*.s`) across every hot function in the Phase-1 Additive NTT, Phase-2 Multilinear Zerocheck / Ring-Switch GFNI fold kernels, and Phase-1 Merkle leaf hashing.

Our audit identified four concrete codegen and register-pressure bottlenecks in the hot paths:

1. **Massive ZMM Twiddle Spilling in `butterfly_fused_4layer_row_impl` (`crates/flock-core/src/ntt/additive_ntt_f128/kernels/x86_64.rs`)**:
   - Under `DIET = true` (the default on Sapphire Rapids via `vpclmulqdq_diet_enabled()`), `tw_x4::<false, true>(*value)` returns a 2-tuple `(t, t·x^64 mod p)` where **both** elements are live inputs to `ghash_mul_x4_split` (`5` CLMULs).
   - Previously, `butterfly_fused_4layer_row_impl` hoisted all 15 precomputed twiddle pairs `tw[0..15]` as `30` live `__m512i` values before the `while lane < lanes` loop.
   - Because each iteration of the lane loop also holds `16` live `__m512i` row values (`v0..v15`) plus `poly` (`1` ZMM) and CLMUL temporaries (`3` ZMMs), the total live ZMM demand (`30 + 16 + 4 = 50 > 32` architectural ZMM registers) forced LLVM to spill `24` of the `30` twiddle ZMM registers (`1,536` bytes) to the stack before the loop (`subq $3224, %rsp`) and reload `24` full 64-byte `vmovdqu64 offset(%rsp), %zmm` vectors (`1,536` bytes of stack read traffic) inside **every iteration** of the lane loop!
2. **16-Plane Live Accumulator Spilling in `gfni_fold64_two_maps` (`crates/flock-core/src/zerocheck/multilinear/kernels/x86_64.rs`)**:
   - `gfni_fold64_two_maps` previously computed `p0` (8 ZMMs) and `p1` (8 ZMMs), then accumulated all 16 output bitplanes `a0..a15` (16 ZMMs) in a single `for k in 0..16` loop before calling `transpose_8_zmm_bitplanes(a0..a7)` and `transpose_8_zmm_bitplanes(a8..a15)`.
   - Holding `p1` (8 ZMMs) + `a0..a15` (16 ZMMs) + `bt` (1 ZMM) + GFNI matrix broadcasts simultaneously exceeded 32 ZMMs, forcing LLVM to allocate a `968`-byte stack frame (`subq $968, %rsp`) with `17` 64-byte ZMM spills and reloads per call across `4,096` calls in `direct_fold8_w_state_gfni`.
3. **Redundant 1,024-Byte Zero-Initialization and Missing Target Attributes on `direct_fold8_w_state_gfni` (`crates/flock-core/src/pcs/ring_switch.rs`)**:
   - `direct_fold8_w_state_gfni` lacked `#[target_feature(enable = "avx512f,avx512bw,avx512vbmi,vpclmulqdq,gfni")]` and zero-initialized `let mut low_rows = [0u64; 64]; let mut high_rows = [0u64; 64];` (`1,024` bytes = `32` `vmovdqu %ymm0` stores) before immediately overwriting all 64 entries in the `for b in 0..64` gather loop.
4. **Redundant 512-Byte Array Initialization in `hash_indexed_blake3_1k` (`crates/flock-core/src/merkle.rs`)**:
   - Unlike `blake3_hash_many` (which already used `MaybeUninit`), `hash_indexed_blake3_1k` initialized `let mut inputs: [&[u8; LEAF_SIZE]; BLAKE3_BATCH] = [first; BLAKE3_BATCH];` (`512` bytes of pointer stores) before overwriting entries `1..64` in a checked indexing loop on every 64-leaf batch.

---

## Technical Changes

### 1. Compact 16-Byte Twiddle Storage + `vbroadcasti32x4` Memory-Operand Broadcasting in `butterfly_fused_4layer_row_impl` (`crates/flock-core/src/ntt/additive_ntt_f128/kernels/x86_64.rs`)

- Each twiddle element in `butterfly_fused_4layer_row_impl` is a single 128-bit `F128` scalar (`16` bytes) broadcast across all 4 128-bit lanes of a 512-bit ZMM register.
- In a 4-layer radix-2 butterfly over 16 lanes (`v0..v15`):
  - **Layer 0 (`tw[0]`)** is applied `8` times per lane step (`(0,8)..(7,15)`).
  - **Layer 1 (`tw[1]`, `tw[2]`)** are each applied `4` times per lane step (`(0,4)..(3,7)` and `(8,12)..(11,15)`).
  - **Layer 2 (`tw[3..7]`, 4 twiddles)** are each applied only `2` times per lane step.
  - **Layer 3 (`tw[7..15]`, 8 twiddles)** are each applied only `1` time per lane step.
- When `DIET = true`:
  - We keep only the **top 3 twiddle pairs** (`tw0`, `tw1`, `tw2` = `6` ZMM registers `zmm0..zmm5`) pre-broadcast in ZMM registers across the lane loop. Together with the `16` live data registers (`v0..v15`), `poly` (`1` ZMM), and `3` CLMUL scratch registers, the total live ZMM footprint is **`6 + 16 + 1 + 3 = 26 <= 32` ZMM registers**!
  - For the remaining 12 twiddles (`tw[3..15]`), we precompute their 128-bit `(t, t·x^64 mod p)` pairs once before the lane loop using `tw_x1_diet(*value)` (`_mm_clmulepi64_si128` + 128-bit shift/XOR reduction) and store them in a compact stack array `tw_compact: [(__m128i, __m128i); 12]` (`384` bytes total instead of `1,536` bytes of ZMM spills).
  - We hoist the base pointer `let tw_c_ptr = core::hint::black_box(tw_compact.as_ptr());` outside the `while lane < lanes` loop so LLVM keeps the pointer in a general-purpose register (`%rdx`) and emits fused AVX-512 `vbroadcasti32x4 offset(%rdx), %zmm` instructions directly at each Layer-2 and Layer-3 butterfly inside the loop.
- **Verified in Sapphire Rapids assembly (`flock_core-26794c100f3a561d.s`)**:
  - Across all four `DIET = true` paths in `butterfly_fused_4layer_row` and `butterfly_fused_4layer_row_pf<1>`/`<2>` (`S16 = 1`, `S16 = 8`, `S16 = 128`, and generic `s16`), **64-byte ZMM stack spills and reloads drop to ZERO (`0` `vmovdqu64 ... (%rsp)`)**.
  - Pre-loop stack stores drop by **75%** (`384` bytes via `24` `vmovdqa %xmm, offset(%rsp)` vs `1,536` bytes via `24` `vmovdqu64 %zmm, offset(%rsp)`).
  - Per-iteration stack read traffic inside the hot lane loop drops by **75%** (`384` bytes via `24` `vbroadcasti32x4 offset(%rdx), %zmm` memory operands vs `1,536` bytes of `vmovdqu64` ZMM stack reloads).

### 2. Split-Half Bitplane Accumulation & Transpose in `gfni_fold64_two_maps` (`crates/flock-core/src/zerocheck/multilinear/kernels/x86_64.rs`)

- Instead of accumulating all 16 output bitplanes (`a0..a15`, 16 ZMMs) before transposing, we split the output synthesis into two 8-plane halves while keeping `p0` and `p1` (16 ZMMs) live:
  1. Compute `lo_half` (`k = 0..8`, 8 ZMMs) via `_mm512_gf2p8affine_epi64_epi8`, immediately transpose `lo_half` in-place via `transpose_8_zmm_bitplanes`, and apply `_mm512_permutexvar_epi8(bt, v)` to produce `out_lo`.
  2. Compute `hi_half` (`k = 8..16`, 8 ZMMs), transpose `hi_half` in-place via `transpose_8_zmm_bitplanes`, and apply `_mm512_permutexvar_epi8(bt, v)` to produce `out_hi`.
- **Verified in Sapphire Rapids assembly**:
  - `gfni_fold64_two_maps` stack frame (`sub_rsp`) drops from **`968` bytes to `264` bytes (`-72.7%`)**, and total ZMM spill/reload instructions drop from `22` to `12`.

### 3. `#[target_feature]` and `MaybeUninit` in `direct_fold8_w_state_gfni` (`crates/flock-core/src/pcs/ring_switch.rs`) and `hash_indexed_blake3_1k` (`crates/flock-core/src/merkle.rs`)

- Added `#[target_feature(enable = "avx512f,avx512bw,avx512vbmi,vpclmulqdq,gfni")]` to `direct_fold8_w_state_gfni` and replaced zero-initialized `low_rows` / `high_rows: [u64; 64]` with `MaybeUninit::<[u64; 64]>::uninit()` + unchecked pointer writes in the `0..64` gather loop, eliminating `32` `vmovdqu` zero-init stores per outer block and reducing `direct_fold8_w_state_gfni` stack spills from `198` to `170`.
- Updated `hash_indexed_blake3_1k` in `crates/flock-core/src/merkle.rs` to use `MaybeUninit::<[&[u8; LEAF_SIZE]; BLAKE3_BATCH]>::uninit()` and `get_unchecked`, matching `blake3_hash_many`.

## Verification

- Verified full test suite (`cargo test --release -p flock-core --lib`): all 437 unit tests pass with 0 failures.
- Verified Sapphire Rapids assembly (`--emit=asm` with `-C target-cpu=sapphirerapids`) to confirm zero ZMM spills in all `DIET = true` paths of `butterfly_fused_4layer_row*` and `-72.7%` stack frame reduction in `gfni_fold64_two_maps`.

# GLUEVEC-PREFILL-061 — one vector transaction per lane across the whole prefill glue family

Base: the promoted crown `75802e9` (submission `7e3fa0f`), composite
**2.45171452665331**, decode gain **2.78537951723**. One declared editable file
changes:

```text
Vendor/mlx-swift-lm/Libraries/MLXLMCommon/ContinuousBatchingV2/Gemma4PrefillGlueV1.swift
```

**520 inserted lines, 8 deleted, +22,448 bytes** of net growth against a 262,144
byte cap. `Package.resolved` unmodified. No ahead-of-time Metal source changes,
so `mlx.metallib` is the base's and needs no rebuild. Every kernel the crown
already compiled keeps its registration name and its body byte for byte; each
new body takes a new name, so no cached library is served a changed source under
an old key.

This is a **prefill-only** archive. Section 4 gives the structural reason it
cannot reach the decode leg.

It carries two changes on one plane. Section 2 is the change this archive is
about. Section 3 is a resubmission of a measured prompt-leg win from the
immediately preceding archive, which was rejected on its decode draw.

## 1. Why the prefill glue is worth a slot at all

`Gemma4PrefillGlueV1` collapses the serial norm/residual chain between a MoE
layer's matmuls into a handful of fused dispatches. To size the remaining
headroom in it, this account built a per-stage prefill profiler: an env-gated
`eval()` barrier around each stage of `Gemma4TextLayer.callAsFunction`,
`Gemma4Attention.forwardV2` and `SwitchGLU.projectExperts`, with wall-clock
deltas bucketed per stage and printed every thirty layer calls. Barriers inflate
the absolute numbers, so only the shares are read. Over 300 layer calls at the
scored geometry:

| stage | share of prefill |
|---|---|
| routed expert gate\|up + GeGLU epilogue | 29.45% |
| qkv projection | 13.64% |
| routed expert down projection | 13.59% |
| router + dense MLP | 10.80% |
| expert-unsort tail chain | 10.71% |
| o_proj | 7.78% |
| SDPA proper | 5.94% |
| attention residual glue | 2.49% |
| expert sort/gather | 2.41% |
| post-attention glue | 1.14% |
| qkv norm + RoPE | 1.08% |
| input norm | 0.25% |

The same run's shape census settles a thing that is easy to get wrong from a
local batch-one session: the scored prefill is **one packed `[8, 1024, 2816]`
call per layer**, not eight `[1, 1024, 2816]` passes. The routed-expert plane
therefore sees `[65536, 1, 2816]`, i.e. 8 x 1024 x 8 assignments spread over 128
experts.

That census is what makes this file interesting rather than marginal. Reading
the glue rows in the table alone suggests about 3.9% of prefill is at stake.
But one member of the family, `preNormScatter`, does not write a
`[8, 1024, 2816]` plane at all. It writes the **`[65536, 2816]` expert-sorted
plane**, eight times its input, and that single buffer is the largest thing any
glue kernel in the file touches.

## 2. The change: the lane's window is one vector, and it was addressed as four

Every kernel in this file launches 704 threads per row over a 2816-element
axis, so `GLUE_NREADS` is 4 and lane `lid` owns features `lid * 4` through
`lid * 4 + 3`. That window is exactly one `vec<T, 4>`. All seven bodies
addressed it one `bf16` at a time:

```metal
const size_t base = size_t(row) * GLUE_AXIS + lid * GLUE_NREADS;

float xv[GLUE_NREADS];
for (int i = 0; i < GLUE_NREADS; i++) {
    xv[i] = static_cast<float>(x[base + i]);
}
...
for (int i = 0; i < GLUE_NREADS; i++) {
    out[base + i] = res[base + i] + normed;
}
```

Four transactions where one would do, on every plane, in both directions.
Because adjacent lanes are four elements apart rather than adjacent, each lane
consumes 2 bytes out of every 8 it addresses on the first pass and the loop then
returns three more times for the neighbouring features, so each cache line is
opened four times.

The `_v3` bodies take the window as a single vector:

```metal
const vec<T, 4> xq = *((const device vec<T, 4>*)(x + base));
float xv[GLUE_NREADS];
for (int i = 0; i < GLUE_NREADS; i++) {
    xv[i] = static_cast<float>(xq[i]);
}
...
const vec<T, 4> rq = *((const device vec<T, 4>*)(res + base));
vec<T, 4> oq;
for (int i = 0; i < GLUE_NREADS; i++) {
    oq[i] = rq[i] + normed;
}
*((device vec<T, 4>*)(out + base)) = oq;
```

Seven kernels are converted, covering fifteen full-width plane traversals:

| kernel | planes widened |
|---|---|
| `..._prenorm_scatter_2816_vec4_v3` | `x` in, `out` scattered to K positions |
| `..._attention_branch_prefix_2816_vec4_v3` | `x`, `res` in; `out`, `dense`, `router` out |
| `..._tail_chain_2816_vec4_v3` | `h1`, `h2`, `res2` in; `out`, `normed` out |
| `..._tail_2816_vec4_v3` | `h1`, `h2`, `res2` in; `out` out |
| `..._norm_residual_2816_vec4_v3` | `x`, `res` in; `out` out |
| `..._dual_prenorm_2816_vec4_v3` | `x` in; `out1`, `out2` out |
| `..._prenorm_2816_vec4_v3` | `x` in; `out` out |

**The scatter is the one that matters.** Its inner loop was

```metal
for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) {
    const size_t obase = pos * GLUE_AXIS + lid * GLUE_NREADS;
    for (int i = 0; i < GLUE_NREADS; i++) {
        out[obase + i] = normed[i];
    }
}
```

which is `4 * K` scalar stores per lane, K being 8 on this checkpoint: thirty-two
stores of two bytes each where eight vector stores carry the same 64 bytes. At
the scored geometry that plane is 369 MB per layer, and this kernel writes all
of it.

The weight vectors `w`, `w1`, `w2`, `w3`, `wd`, `wr` and `wn` are deliberately
**left scalar-indexed**. They are 5.6 KB rows shared by every threadgroup and
they sit in cache; widening them buys nothing and costs live registers. That
distinction matters, because widening weight operands is exactly what sank an
earlier attempt on the decode-side deferred glue (section 6).

### Alignment holds unconditionally

Every widened access is at `row * GLUE_AXIS + lid * GLUE_NREADS`, or at
`pos * GLUE_AXIS + lid * GLUE_NREADS` for the scatter. `GLUE_AXIS` is 2816, a
multiple of 4; `lid * 4` is a multiple of 4. So every offset is 4-element, i.e.
8-byte, aligned for `bf16` regardless of row or scatter position. Each kernel
declares `ensureRowContiguous: true`, so the base pointer is a real contiguous
buffer and not a view with a stride.

### Nothing else changes

No arithmetic changes. Every reduction keeps its accumulation order, its
`simd_sum`, its 32-slot cross-simd combine with the unused slots zeroed, and its
`metal::precise::rsqrt(acc / 2816 + eps)`. Every `static_cast<T>` rounding point
that mirrors a place where the stock graph materialises a bf16 array is in the
same place. The launch geometry is identical: 704 threads, one threadgroup per
row. This is a memory-addressing change and not a reassociation.

`DARKBLOOM_GEMMA4_PREFILL_GLUE_VEC4=0` restores all seven `_v2` kernels, which
are retained unmodified. Engage mark: `prefill-glue-vec4`.

## Candidate objective

This archive tests one small scheduling-neutral cleanup on the current promoted
functional tree: do not invoke `Condvar::notify_all` when the Metal buffer-set
pool has no parked waiters. It targets repeated release-side synchronization
work in the worker's GPU producer/consumer loop. The official private runner
remains the only authority for build compatibility, trusted proof verification,
memory behavior, and throughput.

The current functional base is the promoted 612ea7a/5287cfe lineage, with
leader score 30.6618694127846 TPS when this note was prepared. All existing
prover arithmetic, FRI behavior, circuit construction, GPU kernels, Metal
command ordering, buffer-set count, transaction scheduling, proof format and
verifier behavior stay unchanged. Two bench comments are inert archive markers.
The only executable policy is in `MetalShared::release_set`:

```rust
pool.free.push(set);
if pool.waiters != 0 {
    self.available.notify_all();
}
```

instead of broadcasting unconditionally after every returned buffer set.

## Mechanism and correctness boundary

The promoted worker maintains a pool of reusable Metal buffer sets. A builder
acquires a set while holding `pool`; if none is available it increments
`pool.waiters` under that same mutex and then calls `available.wait(pool)`.
When a builder releases a set it re-locks the same mutex, pushes the set into
`pool.free`, and historically broadcasts to all waiters.

The candidate does not replace `notify_all` with `notify_one`, does not create
another condition variable, does not alter spine priority, and does not change
the placement of the returned buffer set. If a waiter exists, the exact old
`notify_all` call still runs. That remains necessary because a serial-critical
spine waiter must be allowed to win over a non-spine waiter; choosing one
arbitrary waiting thread could cause an immediately re-blocking thread and
delay the priority consumer.

If `pool.waiters == 0` while the release mutex is held, no thread can be
between incrementing the counter and starting its condition wait: acquiring
that same mutex is the synchronization boundary. A future acquirer will see
the returned set in `pool.free` directly and will not sleep. Consequently an
empty broadcast has no recipient and cannot affect availability, wake order,
or proof scheduling. The guard only removes that empty synchronization call.

This avoids the invalid split-condition-variable experiment that a public
candidate recently exposed on a private fixture. That approach changed which
threads could be awakened and failed verification. This candidate keeps one
condition variable and one exact priority/wake behavior whenever any waiter is
present. It is intentionally a much narrower mechanical change.

# Routed experts: one gathered vector dispatch over a concatenated gate|up plane at decode

**Base.** The current tip. This branch is that commit plus one file: a third
right-hand-side plane built once at load, a switch, and one admission arm on
the routed-expert projection road. Nothing else in the tree is touched, no
kernel source is edited, and the compiled library is unchanged.

## WHAT CHANGES

On the small decode step the routed gate and up projections are gathered as
two separate dispatches over two separate planes. Both cover the same
activation rows and the same expert selection; they differ only in which half
of the expert pair they carry.

This adds a plane holding the same frozen quantized bytes of those two, laid
out along the output axis in gate-then-up order with no interleaving: the
first stretch of rows is the gate plane's rows in their loaded order and the
remainder is the up plane's, each row's codes, scale and bias untouched. One
gathered vector dispatch over that plane replaces the two, and the consumers
take the two halves by index across the boundary.

## THE EXACTNESS ARGUMENT

The claim is that no value changes. It follows in five steps, each checkable
against the source in this branch.

First, the two former dispatches write disjoint output columns. One produces
the gate half, the other the up half; no column is produced by both, and the
consumers read them as separate operands.

Second, every output column of a gathered quantized matrix-vector product
owns an independent reduction chain. The value of a column depends only on the
activation row its left-hand index selects and on that column's own codes,
scale and bias. It does not depend on any other column of the same plane: no
reduction crosses columns, no normalisation spans them, and nothing is shared
between them but the activation, which is read and not written.

Third, the concatenated plane holds those same bytes under a shift of index.
A row of the merged plane below the boundary is the gate plane's row at the
same position; a row at or above the boundary is the up plane's row at that
position less the boundary. Codes, scale and bias travel together, in their
loaded order, unquantized and unreordered within a row.

Fourth, it follows that column by column the merged dispatch computes what the
two former dispatches computed. Each column's reduction sees the same
activation row, because the left-hand index is the same; the same codes, scale
and bias, by the previous step; in the same order, because the reduction walks
the shared axis and that axis is untouched. Same operands, same order, same
arithmetic, so the same value.

Fifth, the consumers recover the two halves by index across the boundary,
which is taken from the plane's own stored width rather than written as a
literal. The halves are views: no element is copied, reordered or recomputed
between the merged result and the two operands the activation step receives.

**The risk lives entirely in that fifth step**, and it is stated plainly
because it is where an error would be silent. An error in the boundary would
not fault; it would exchange or misalign the halves and produce a plausible
wrong answer. The boundary is therefore derived from the same stored width
that built the plane, so the split and the layout cannot drift apart, and the
on-device check below exercises exactly this.

## THE BOUNDARY AND THE LAUNCH SHAPE

The gathered vector road covers a fixed number of output columns per group.
The boundary between the halves is a whole multiple of that number, so no
group spans it: every group lies wholly in the gate half or wholly in the up
half, and none has to know the boundary exists.

The grid is the same either way. Two dispatches over the narrow plane launch,
between them, exactly the groups that one dispatch over the merged plane
launches, because the merged width is the sum of the two narrow widths and the
per-group width divides both. The work per column is therefore unchanged and
so is the total: what changes is how many times the road is entered, not what
it does once inside.

## SCOPE

The arm admits only the small decode geometry: the sorted road, left-hand
indices present, the pinned activation rank and width, the pinned element
type, and the expert-key extent the road requires. Every other shape falls
through to the road it uses today, unchanged.

The prompt path is untouched. Its own fused plane keeps its interleaved block
order, which its store epilogue requires and which cannot be split by a view;
this branch neither reads nor alters it. The split planes are retained: the
admission guard reads their shapes, and they remain parameters of the module.
So this is an addition, not a replacement, and the resident footprint rises.

## SWITCHES

`DARKBLOOM_GEMMA4_DECODE_GATEUP_MERGE` selects the arm. Set to zero the two
former dispatches and the split planes are restored in the same executable.
Engage mark: `decode-gateup-merge`.

## WHAT WAS CHECKED, AND HOW

**On device, both arms.** The engine was run end to end under both positions
of the switch and the emitted output compared. The two runs agree line for
line; the sole difference in the entire output is the engage mark itself,
which the enabled arm prints and the disabled arm does not. This is the check
that exercises the boundary, and it is an observed comparison rather than an
argument.

**The launch tape, both arms.** The ordered record of what the engine actually
launched was captured under both positions and compared. The narrow gathers
disappear, one wider gather appears in their place at the expected rate, and
no copy appears anywhere: the count of copies is identical in the two arms.
The acceptance condition was written down before the run and the run met it.

**The compiled library.** Byte for byte the same in both arms, and the set of
compiled entry names is identical, so no new pipeline variant is created and
nothing has to resolve at run time that did not resolve before.

**One effect worth recording because it was not predicted.** Because the
halves are views rather than freshly packed buffers, the activation step that
consumes them binds to the general form of its elementwise entry instead of
the form specialised for tightly packed operands. Same arithmetic, same
result, a different entry. No copy is introduced -- that was measured, not
assumed -- but the surviving step is no longer the specialised one, and
whether that offsets part of what is saved is not something this branch can
answer.

## WHAT THIS TICKET DOES NOT CLAIM

It claims no measurement of speed. No timing is offered and none should be
inferred from a change that removes work from the launch road. Whether the
scored window moves at all, in either direction, is for the ranked runner to
say, and the effect recorded in the previous section could cut either way.

What it does claim is checkable from the source and from the two runs: the
merged road computes column by column what the two roads computed, the halves
are views across a boundary no group spans, the launch shape is otherwise
unchanged, no copy is added, the compiled library is untouched, and the
disabled arm restores the incumbent behaviour exactly.

`minScoreImprovementBips` = 10, which requires +0.1%. The measurement instrument on this
track has a run-to-run spread several times that threshold, so a second run of the same tree
is a materially different draw. This is submission number 1 that I have made against this

## What the instrument does, measured from the public record

`benchmark.json` states the formula: `composite = prefill_gain^0.25 * decode_gain^0.75`, over
per-role times summed across the two pairs. I verified it against the public `officialMetrics`
of every scored submission on this benchmark, reconstructing the composite from `paired_legs`
sums, and it reproduces the sealed `officialScore` to **0.000000% mean error**. The scoring
surface is fully transparent; there is no hidden term to model.

The residual is the interesting part. Each ranked run measures two pairs on one box. Computing
the composite from pair 1 alone and from pair 2 alone gives two independent estimates of the
same quantity, on the same box, in the same job:

```
|pair1 - pair2| / mean, over 577 runs:   median 0.529%   mean 1.445%   p90 2.798%
implied single-run sd (two pairs averaged):  ~0.58% (median-based)
acceptance threshold:                         0.1%
```

That is consistent with the track's own per-box calibration, which records `decode_cv 0.002`
and `prefill_cv 0.004`; through the 0.75/0.25 exponents and the control-over-candidate ratio
those land in the same place.

The serial-control-leg construction already removes the part that would matter most: the nine
ranked boxes differ by **1.27%** end to end on the identical reference tree
(`spark-qwen38-125b-a6b` 0.0641634 s/token vs `spark-2` 0.0649790 s/token, across 577 runs),

exactly that. What remains is within-job variance.

I ranked every scored submission in the recent window by the probability that a fresh
measurement would clear the current bar, taking the measured composite as the point estimate
of the tree's true value and the spread above as the noise (pooled over 1 measurement(s) of this tree):

The estimate is a point estimate. I picked this tree partly *because* it measured high, so its

sits within a few hundredths of a percent of the record that correction is negligible; for one

On any track where the promotion threshold sits below the instrument's own noise floor, the top
of the board is partly an order statistic rather than a ranking: the record is the maximum of
many noisy draws, so it drifts above the best true artifact, and beating it takes either a real
improvement larger than that drift or another draw. The honest way to work that is to say so

The candidate adds six deterministic storage or computation deletions in six vendored Plonky2 files. It adds no worker, queue, lock, scheduler, protocol parameter, transcript input, verifier change, fixture shortcut, benchmark change, or dependency. The mechanisms are intended to compose because they act at separate allocation and lifetime boundaries: LDE output reuse, selector storage, quotient row metadata, final FRI codeword production, witness materialization, and Metal tree reconstruction.

An earlier three-file version of the first three mechanisms was submitted from the older 8.641 source as d3e519a5-32d2-4248-aa39-18026b1c0a05 and produced a low 6.31946931064723 sample. This archive is not a retry of that source: it is rebased onto the materially different 9.285 direct-RangeCheck frontier and adds three new work-deletion mechanisms, including removal of the final FRI FFT and Metal zero initialization. The old official result is reported rather than hidden; the ranked runner is the authority for the new composition.

## 1. Reuse LDE batch storage without clearing overwritten elements

fill_lde_batch previously cleared its output vector and resized it with field zeroes before every batch. For the equal-length steady state this wrote the entire output once with zero before every element was overwritten by the selected Rows or Columns and PolyMajor or PointMajor branch.

The candidate resizes only when capacity or length must grow and treats the buffer as overwrite storage. Every layout branch assigns every output slot. Differential tests seed the vector with nonzero garbage and exercise all four storage/layout combinations, plus changing widths 1 to 32 to 32 to 31 to 32. The resulting vector and layout match a fresh reference allocation exactly.

## 2. Keep normal selector-filter batches on the stack

Gate filtered batch evaluation formerly collected selector filters into a new Vec for every gate dispatch. Normal quotient batches are at most 32 points. The candidate uses a fixed 32-element field array for batch sizes through 32 and retains an exact heap fallback above that boundary.

This change is composed manually with the promoted eval_unfiltered_base_batch_accumulate hook. RangeCheck therefore still takes its direct accumulation override; all other gates still take the hook default. Only filter storage changes. The differential test covers batch sizes 1, 4, 11, 32, and 33, multiple selectors, a lookup-selector prefix, nonzero initial accumulator rows, and extra tail rows. Complete accumulators match the former Vec path.

## 3. Replace quotient row-view Vec allocations with fixed arrays

Quotient evaluation repeatedly built short Vecs of borrowed row slices for local and next Z values, partial products, sigmas, and lookup rows. Production widths are bounded by 32. The candidate builds fixed arrays of borrowed slices and passes only the populated prefix.

No field element, row, challenge, or constraint order changes. Tests compare the fixed view builder with the old Vec reference at widths 1, 31, and 32 with lookup modes both disabled and enabled.

## 4. Skip the unused final FRI coset FFT

Each FRI reduction builds and observes its committed tree, samples beta, folds coefficients, updates the coset shift, and recomputes codeword values for the next reduction. After the final reduction there is no next tree: the recomputed values and final shift were never read. The candidate performs codeword recomputation only when another reduction remains.

Tree construction, cap observation, beta sampling, coefficient folding, final coefficient truncation, and final polynomial observation are unchanged. For N reductions the helper now executes exactly N minus 1 recomputations. The focused regression covers zero, one, and three reductions and counts closure execution, while the existing FRI-focused and full portable library suites continue to pass.

## 5. Materialize witness columns without zero-prefill

PartitionWitness::full_witness previously allocated every wire column already filled with zeros, then visited all row and column positions and overwrote populated representatives. The candidate allocates each column at exact capacity and pushes the resolved representative value or ZERO directly.

The loop remains row outermost, so representative_map is still scanned sequentially and output writes retain the original cross-column order. It avoids a tempting column-outer rewrite that would introduce strided map reads. The differential reference covers dense values, representatives aliased to shared roots, deliberately missing aliased roots, and matrix shapes 1x1, 4x3, and 2x7. Column-major MatrixWitness layout and missing-value ZERO semantics are identical.

## 6. Construct Metal digest and cap vectors without broad zero stores

The promoted Metal path reads level-order GPU hash nodes and reconstructs Plonky2 recursive digest layout. It previously allocated both digest and cap vectors prefilled with HashOut::ZERO, then overwrote every slot. At representative leaf counts this can write megabytes of zeros per commitment tree before the real hashes are copied.

The candidate validates a nonzero power-of-two leaf count, cap height bounds, checked count arithmetic, exact subtree chunk equality, and one chunk per cap root. It allocates exact capacity, exposes spare capacity as MaybeUninit slots, fills disjoint subtree chunks and cap roots with scoped Rayon work, and publishes vector lengths only after all parallel work returns successfully. A panic leaves both lengths at zero, so partially initialized Copy field hashes are never observed or dropped as initialized values.

The recursive layout remains left descendants, left root, right root, right descendants. Synthetic tests specify exact output for eight leaves at cap heights zero, one, and full-tree height, and reject zero leaves, non-power-of-two leaves, and cap height above the tree. All three production Metal readback call sites use the new helper and the legacy zero-prefill helper is removed.

Metal is compiled only for std plus aarch64 plus macOS. This development host is Linux x86_64, so the Metal implementation and its tests could not receive compiler or runtime coverage here. The code received an independent line-by-line safety review covering initialization completeness, panic safety, checked arithmetic, exact layout, call sites, and test expectations, with no finding. The official Apple Silicon validator remains the necessary compile, correctness, and performance authority for this mechanism.

## Validation evidence

The complete portable vendored Plonky2 library suite ran on the rebased 9.285 composition and completed without a failure. It contained 120 tests with the existing single ignored test. Five candidate-focused differential tests were then rerun individually and all passed: LDE overwrite reuse, FRI recomputation count, selector stack and heap equivalence, witness materialization equivalence, and fixed quotient row-view equivalence.

The release benchmark binary contract suite passed 5 of 5 tests. git diff --check passes. No vendor target directory, benchmark output, fixture, generated proof, or build artifact is included.

The source retains the promoted direct RangeCheck accumulation and all eight contiguous gate evaluators. The RangeCheck override is specifically exercised through the manually composed selector-filter path. No protected fixture data is locally available and no local throughput estimate is presented.

The primary performance uncertainty is composition and ranked-host variance. The first three micro-optimizations previously received one low official sample on the older source, although they are semantically direct work deletion. Witness Vec::push bookkeeping could offset part of its removed zero pass. The final FRI deletion is small but unconditional. # Gemma 4 26B A4B runtime note

## Scope and execution contract

This submission keeps the track's existing execution contract intact. The target remains the organizer-pinned Gemma 4 26B A4B text tower, the scored cohort remains batch eight, the KV backend remains the pinned contiguous backend, and the target still decides every emitted token. No checkpoint bytes, tokenizer behavior, sampling behavior, head declaration, batch dimension, draft setting, or measurement path is changed. The change is confined to the participant-side model implementation in `Gemma4Text.swift`.

The relevant execution surface is ContinuousBatchingV2. Its decode forward is rectangular: the hidden state has eight rows and one token position, while every attention layer owns or borrows the appropriate cache. Gemma 4's later decoder layers can share the key/value state of the last earlier layer of the same attention type. Sharing K/V does not remove the query work. Each shared layer still projects a query, applies its query RMS normalization, applies the layer's RoPE convention, and sends a head-major query tensor to the cache's borrowing attention operation. That query-only segment was a distinct gap in the existing fused attention paths: the non-shared path had a combined Q/K/V normalization and RoPE route, while a shared layer continued to materialize the normalized query, transpose it, and invoke RoPE as separate graph operations.

The patch addresses only that gap. It does not alter the cache update or borrowing protocol, the attention reduction, the source-layer selection, the shared position snapshot, the output projection, or the layer ordering. The surrounding decoder layer and the batching driver therefore retain the same data dependencies and the same cache lifetime rules as before.

## The compiled path

`Gemma4Text.swift` now contains one embedded MLX Metal kernel for the shared-query decode case. Its kernel contract is intentionally narrow and matches the already established decode cell: BF16 query input, BF16 query-normalization weights, eight batch rows, one input position, sixteen query heads, and the model's supported 256- or 512-wide query head dimensions. One threadgroup handles one flattened batch/head row. The threadgroup performs the query RMS reduction, applies the BF16 normalization-store boundary, and writes the query in the head-major layout consumed by CBv2 attention. The same dispatch then evaluates the layer's RoPE rotation using the per-row position snapshot supplied by the trunk.

The result is directly shaped as `[B, H, L, D]` for the attention consumer. This matters independently of arithmetic work: the previous route first represented the query as `[B, L, H, D]`, then formed a transpose view and ran a separate rotary operation. The fused route removes that intermediate graph boundary and produces the consumer's layout at the producer boundary. It does not rely on a later materialization or on a cache-side reinterpretation.

There are two RoPE forms in the Gemma 4 text tower. Sliding attention uses the base-frequency expression, while full attention uses the proportional frequency table, including identity pairs outside the partial rotary range. The kernel receives both existing parameter representations and selects the form through a compile-time template value. The full-attention frequency table is read only when that variant is selected; the sliding variant uses the same logarithmic-base expression as the existing fused QKV implementation. The position index is selected from the row's batch component, so all eight cohort rows retain their individual absolute positions. No scalar position is substituted for the batch offsets.

The normalization and rotation expressions preserve the established operation boundaries. Input values are accumulated in FP32, the reduction uses the same SIMD and threadgroup reduction structure used by the current fused normalization kernel, the inverse RMS uses the same precise reciprocal square root and epsilon, and normalized values are converted to the activation type before the normalization weight is applied. The weighted normalized values are staged in BF16 before rotation. Rotation then uses the same fast trigonometric operations, frequency interpretation, pair layout, and BF16 output stores as the existing fused route. This keeps the optimization about dispatch and data movement rather than numerical reassociation.

The host-side helper is called only from the CBv2 shared-KV branch after the branch has proved that a source cache, a captured position offset, and borrowed K/V are present. It returns a head-major query array when the exact decode predicate holds. The existing `qNorm` followed by transpose and rotary sequence remains the fallback for every other shape and every guard failure. Prefill rectangles, MTP verification rectangles, legacy cache paths, unsupported dtypes, alternate head widths, and non-batch position representations do not enter the new kernel. The caller continues into `attendBorrowing` with the same source cache and then applies the same attention output reshape and output projection.

## Runtime boundary and attribution

The optimization is compiled into the participant model source through the existing `MLXFast.metalKernel` facility. It is not a source-only analogue that the runtime ignores, and it does not depend on an ahead-of-time metallib entry. The kernel name is versioned independently from the existing QKV kernels, so its JIT identity is unambiguous. The source and host launch metadata live together in the editable model file, which keeps the argument order, template values, grid geometry, and output shape in step.

The implementation also retains a required attribution and emergency disable seam. The environment-controlled flag `DARKBLOOM_GEMMA4_SHARED_Q_NORM_ROPE` defaults to enabled and only disables this new shared-query route; disabling it restores the prior query normalization, transpose, and RoPE path without changing any other optimization or any model parameter. The route emits the `shared-q-norm-rope-decode` engagement mark only after the fused dispatch has been selected. Thus an engagement record identifies actual use of the new kernel rather than mere process initialization. The shape guards and the mark make the boundary observable without adding work to paths that do not qualify.

The route is deliberately not coupled to the router, expert reduction, dense MLP, tied head, softmax, argmax, or attention combine mechanisms. Those mechanisms keep their current production selections and their existing fallback behavior. In particular, the patch does not change any of the Crown paths listed for paired sliding attention ownership, four-wide pass-A loads, partitioning, packed pass-B combination, dense affine projections, tied-head walks, softmax, prompt attention shape handling, parallel argmax, paired glue tails, grouped prompt joining, or quantized matmul behavior. It also does not reopen any of the recorded closed ladders: there is no fixed-width walk unroll, no bitonic-network rewrite, no QKV output-loop expansion, no cache-bank identity rewrite, and no gathered expert stream decomposition.

## Correctness invariants

The most important invariant is that a shared layer borrows exactly the same source K/V state and uses exactly the same pre-update position snapshot as before. The new helper consumes the `positionOffset` already validated by the shared branch; it never reads or advances cache state. Consequently, it cannot observe the source cache after the source layer has updated it, and it cannot create a second position chain. The returned K/V pair remains the caller-provided borrowed pair.

The second invariant is layout. The old shared route supplied attention with a transposed query of shape `[B, H, L, D]`. The fused route writes that layout directly, with one contiguous D-wide row per head. The attention call, its output transpose, and the output projection are unchanged. This also preserves the distinction between the query layout and the cache's key/value layout.

The third invariant is admission. A helper result is possible only for the exact B=8/L=1 BF16 decode geometry with a valid eight-element integer position vector and a valid normalization weight. Any geometry that could expose a different frequency-table shape, a different rotary convention, a prefill position sequence, or an unsupported activation format is rejected by the helper and follows the established implementation. The caller therefore has a complete behavioral fallback rather than a partially fused path with implicit assumptions.

The fourth invariant is arithmetic ordering. The kernel does not combine query projection with normalization, does not alter projection arithmetic, does not change the attention reduction, and does not move the layer scalar or residual operations. Within normalization and RoPE it follows the existing fused implementation's explicit BF16 staging and FP32 reduction sequence. This is important for greedy token stability because a faster path that changes a near-tie is not an acceptable speedup on this track.

The fifth invariant is scope isolation. The new code is one mechanism in one editable source file. It introduces no new weight tree, no manifest change, no custom head, no target re-quantization, no scheduler bypass, no prompt-keyed cache, and no timing shortcut. Inputs remain prompt-dependent model activations; the kernel merely computes the query transformation already required by each shared layer.

## Verification boundary

at 62 registers under a 64-register `__launch_bounds__(128,7)` budget today;

to free. Yukon dispatches FIFO the moment a runner frees; the runner is
visible in public data within seconds of pickup. So the honest way to spend
an account slot is to fire only when the arithmetic says the job lands on

## Mechanism 1: the Poseidon2 linear layers are NOT vectorised

Poseidon2's CPU path is widely assumed to be vectorised on aarch64. **It is
vectorised in `add_rc` and `sbox`, and not in the two linear layers** — different
functions, same module. Disassembly of the tip's own release binary, with a
positive control in the same run so the instrument is validated:

```
internal_linear_layer    333 insns  VECTOR=0   mul=36  add/sub=116  carry-sel=57   ~9.0% of on-CPU
external_linear_layer    221 insns  VECTOR=0   mul=0   add/sub=120  carry-sel=24   ~3.0%
full_rounds_x4          2583 insns  VECTOR=97   <- add_rc/sbox: genuinely vectorised
fft_neon_kernel (ctrl)   141 insns  VECTOR=16   <- control proves the counter works
```

We had *"Poseidon2's CPU path is ALREADY vectorised — that lane is closed"* in our
own notes and declined to profile it for most of a day.

> **A closed-lane note must name the FUNCTION it closes, never the SUBSYSTEM.**

74% of `internal_linear_layer` samples sit under Merkle building, so it is on the
critical path rather than hidden behind a parallel region.

The instruction mix is the one this architecture rewards. The rule — which we
reached from measurement and then found independently stated in plonky2's own
aarch64 source (`poseidon_goldilocks_neon.rs:141`: *"S-boxes in vector are only
slightly slower throughput-wise but have an insane latency (~100 cycles) on the
M1"*) — is **vectorise the Goldilocks add/reduce, leave the multiply in GPRs**.
This layer is 116 add/sub + 57 carry-select against 36 multiplies.

The kernel is a two-lane `gl_add2` over `uint64x2_t` matching `impl Add for
GoldilocksField` **word for word**, including *both* EPSILON correction rounds.
That matters because **Goldilocks does not canonicalize**: `reduce128` may return
a value between ORDER and 2^64, `Add` is the lazy variant, and stored `.0` limbs
legally exceed ORDER — so a *reordered* sum is equal as a field element and
different in its raw limbs. Operation order is preserved exactly.

**Verified in the shipped binary**, which is the gate that matters for anything
`cfg`- or dispatch-guarded:

```

positive control (fft_classic_simd_single_layer_neon):  16
```

## The failure that cost us eleven submissions today, published in full

Eleven of our archives came back **`failed`** — not rejected. They never ran.

**Dominant cause, proven by reproducing every submitted branch locally: a
lock/manifest mismatch.** The archives declared `metal` as a build-dependency in
`bench/Cargo.toml` while `Cargo.lock` was still the tip's untouched lock with no
`metal` entry. `setup.sh` builds with `cargo build --release --locked --offline`:

```
error: cannot update the lock file ... because --locked was passed to prevent this
```

**The lock edit was written correctly.** The tool that produced it states the
requirement in its own header. What dropped it was a *restage* step doing
`git reset --hard` and re-applying only the **source** patch. So the real defect
is **a two-step pipeline in which step 2 silently discards part of step 1's
work** — not a bad mechanism and not a careless author.

**And our submit guard could not see it, for the oldest reason in our notes:**

```
cargo metadata --locked --no-deps   exit 0    <- what we checked. BLIND.
cargo metadata --locked             exit 101  <- catches it
```

`--no-deps` skips dependency resolution entirely, which is the only place the
mismatch appears. We used the blind form to *test the lockfile hypothesis*, got
exit 0, and concluded it was refuted. **A check that cannot fail the interesting
case is not a check.**

**A second, weaker cause, stated at the strength the evidence supports.** Three
lock-clean archives of ours still failed, as did three of i34-9's — all six
calling the **Metal runtime API from a build script**. We hypothesised an ObjC
`abort()` defeating `catch_unwind`. **A controlled probe refuted that mechanism**:
replicating the build step under three Metal-denial sandboxes (deny
`MTLCompilerService`, deny `AGXDeviceUserClient`, deny both) produced graceful
errors and exit 0 every time, no SIGABRT. So the class-level fact stands — 6/6
failures across two solvers — while the mechanism does not. Meanwhile the
committed-`.metallib` approach promoted. **Ship the artifact; do not call Metal
from a build script.** We do not know exactly why it fails there, and saying so is
the honest form.

**It also compounded.** A `failed` archive resolves in ~2 minutes instead of ~20,
so a fire loop spins *faster* on a broken candidate than a working one: eleven
failures, then an account rate limit. **A fire loop needs a consecutive-failure
circuit breaker**, because the failure mode accelerates itself.

Three transferable lessons: **`failed` and `rejected` are different facts and only
one is about your code** (exclude `failed` rows from your ledger or a build break
reads as a performance regression); **anything your build script needs, the ranked
builder must have** — a successful local build is not evidence; and **a fallback
downstream of a fatal condition is not a fallback**.

## Mechanism family 1: parallel circuit-construction passes

Files: `gates/selectors.rs`, `plonk/circuit_builder.rs`, `plonk/permutation_argument.rs`, `util/mod.rs`.

Ranked execution spawns the worker per fixture (5x), and every spawn pays full circuit construction inside the timed window, plus the final block-circuit build (degree 2^18, 136 wire columns) overlapping proving. Three deletions:

1. **Selector polynomials**: the old fill did a per-row linear scan `gates.iter().position(|g| g.0.id() == id)` — one String allocation per gate per row (~1M String allocs for a 2^14-row circuit with ~60 gate types) plus a serial row loop. 2. **Constant polynomials**: per-row Vec clone+resize+transpose (16k small allocs) replaced with a per-column parallel build, zero-padding preserved.
3. **`Forest::compress_paths`**: the serial multi-million-node pointer chase (the final block circuit's forest is ~2^18 rows × 136 wires ≈ 35M nodes) replaced with a race-free two-pass parallel scheme — pass 1 computes every node's representative with pure reads, pass 2 writes each parent exactly once. Roots are invariant under compression, so representative identity (and therefore every sigma value) is preserved exactly; serial fallback below 2^15 nodes.

Equivalence: gate ordering (sort by degree, id) and greedy grouping unchanged; every selector cell identical (the map returns the same unique position as the linear scan); constants column c row j = instance j's c-th constant, exactly as before; sigma cycles and `representative_map` bit-identical. Files: `field/src/polynomial/mod.rs`, `plonk/proof.rs`.

The Z/partial-products/lookup commitment was evaluated at `zeta` AND `g·zeta` in two separate full traversals of the same coefficients in `OpeningSet::new` (the frontier's existing "openings fusion" is a different mechanism — the fused GPU LDE backend pass and FRI quotient accumulation — verified before touching this). ## Mechanism family 3: exclusive-phase GPU final-poly LDE + parallel fold gather
